newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UNITA told to respect Angola pact or face sanctions.
newsitem.headline: UNITA told to respect Angola pact or face sanctions.

text.p: The Security Council expressed concern on Wednesday that the former UNITA rebels in Angola were trying to restore their military capabilities and warned of possible sanctions.

A statement read at a brief public meeting said increasing tension in the northern part of the country was spreading rapidly to the central and southern provinces, "with very dangerous implications for the implementation of the remaining tasks of the peace process."
"The council calls upon both parties to refrain from any use of force," it added.

After two decades of civil war UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, entered into a unity government in April with the ruling MPLA (Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola) but still controls large areas of the country. UNITA fighters should have been demobilized or incorporated into a new national army.

The council statement expressed "deep concern at recent destabilising actions in Angola, in particular the failure of ... UNITA to comply" with the latest U.N. resolution on the peace process "and its continued efforts to restore its military capabilities."

Statements submitted by UNITA regarding the strength of its armed forces, the extension of state administration and the activities of its Vorgan radio station were "neither complete nor credible," the council said.

It reaffirmed its readiness to "consider the imposition of measures," including trade and travel curbs first threatened in 1993, "unless UNITA takes irreversible and concrete steps immediately to fulfil its obligations under the Lusaka Protocol," the 1994 agreement on which the peace process is based.

The council said the steps demanded of UNITA included demilitarization of all its forces, transformation of its radio station into a non-partisan broadcasting facility and full cooperation in normalising state administration throughout the country.

Secretary-General Kofi Annan was asked to inform the council how UNITA was carrying out those tasks in a report he is already due to submit by Aug. 15 on the situation in Angola, where a large U.N. peacekeeping operation is being replaced by a smaller observer mission.

The council also condemned the mistreatment of U.N. personnel and staff of international humanitarian organisations in areas under UNITA control, as well as the harassment of members of the U.N. Observer Mission in Angola (MONUA) in the exercise of their duties.
"Those actions by UNITA are unacceptable and contrary to its commitments under the Lusaka Protocol and to Security Council resolutions," the statement said.

A long-awaited meeting on Angolan territory between President Jose Eduardo dos Santos and UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi "could greatly contribute to the reduction of tension and to the process of national reconciliation," the council added.
